summary: A humorous April 1 memo written as a historical look back at the usage of an imaginary IP version 9. It is a joke, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st RFC presents a fictional history of IP Version 9. It describes imaginary routing levels, address allocation, and connected devices in a straight-faced technical style.

questions: what is the imaginary ip version 9 in rfc 1606
subtitle: A comic future history of an imaginary IP Version 9.

tldr.problem: The memo imagines a future review of a network protocol that is said to be nearing address exhaustion.
tldr.mechanism: It describes a fictional IP Version 9 with a deep routing hierarchy and speculative uses for addressing objects and devices.
tldr.outcome: The imagined protocol's successes and problems form an April 1st satire about network growth and pervasive connectivity.

today: RFC 1606 is an Informational April 1st satire about an imaginary IP Version 9. It does not specify a real protocol.

sections.title: The Imaginary Protocol
sections.content:
The memo pretends that TCP/IPv9 had been widely adopted and was approaching the end of its useful life because of address-space exhaustion. It then reviews the fictional protocol's supposed features and applications.

The author presents the account as a retrospective, while the memo's April 1st publication signals its satirical premise.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is written as a look back at a made-up IP version. Its technical-sounding history is the setup for the satire.

sections.title: Routing and Address Allocation
sections.content:
The imagined IPv9 uses a routing hierarchy of up to 42 levels. The memo describes assigning different levels to parts of devices and proposes that households receive a very large address range that could be divided among rooms and equipment.

It extends the scenario to address needs across planets, galaxies, and parallel universes. These details are part of the fictional future described in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The fictional protocol assigns addresses through many levels, from a whole network down to individual components. The memo pushes that idea into increasingly unlikely settings.

sections.title: Applications in the Fictional Future
sections.content:
The memo imagines IPv9-addressable medical monitors, consumer packaging, magazines, and shoes. It describes concerns such as privacy and interference alongside the absurdity of objects communicating through the network.

It also jokes about manufacturing network devices with biological or nanoscale methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples imagine ordinary products and body monitors connected to the network. Their exaggerated benefits and problems carry the humor of the RFC.
